A reverse entropy power inequality for i.i.d. log-concave random variables

Zhen Fu, and Jiange Li Address: (Z.F, J.L) Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics, Harbin Institute of Technology, China Email address: zhenfu@stu.hit.edu.cn, jiange.li@hit.edu.cn
Abstract.

We show that h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(Z+W)h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(Z+W), where X,YX,Y are independent log-concave random variables, and Z,WZ,W are exponential random variables having the same respective ∞\infty-Rényi entropies. Analogs for integer-valued monotone log-concave random variables are also obtained. Our main tools are decreasing rearrangement, majorization, and the change of measure.

1. Introduction

Let XX be a random vector taking values in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Suppose that it has density ff with respect to the Lebesgue measure. The classical differential entropy (also called Boltzmann-Shannon entropy) of XX is defined as

h(X)=−∫ℝdf(x)logf(x)dx.h(X)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x)\log f(x)dx.

The celebrated entropy power inequality (or EPI for short) of Shannon [18] (and Stam [20]) states that for independent random vectors XX and YY in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that the entropies of X,YX,Y, and X+YX+Y exist, it holds that

e2d​h​(X+Y)≥e2d​h​(X)+e2d​h​(Y),e^{\frac{2}{d}h(X+Y)}\geq e^{\frac{2}{d}h(X)}+e^{\frac{2}{d}h(Y)}, (1.1)

where equality holds if and only if XX and YY are Gaussian random vectors with proportional covariance matrices. The EPI found its original applications in the study of channel capacity in information theory. It has been known very well that EPI is closely related to geometric and functional inequalities in a variety of mathematical fields, maybe most notably the Brunn-Minkowski inequality (or BMI for short) in convex geometry. We refer the interested reader to [7, 12] for profound connections among EPI, BMI, and many other geometric and functional inequalities.

Convexity (or concavity) underpins the validity of the reversal of many geometric and functional inequalities. A function f:ℝd→ℝ+f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is called log-concave if it can be written as f⁡(x)=e−V⁡(x)f(x)=e^{-V(x)}, where V:ℝd→ℝ∪{∞}V:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} is a convex function. We say that a random vector XX taking values in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is log-concave provided that its density is a log-concave function. (We also say that XX has log-concave distribution). The class of log-concave functions can be thought of as functional analogs of convex bodies. They are prominent objects studied in convex geometry, high dimensional probability and statistics, as well as theoretical computer science. The class of log-concave distributions include a wide range of important probability distributions, such as the Gaussian distributions, uniform distributions on convex bodies, and exponential distributions.

The reversal of EPI was first addressed by Bobkov and Madiman [3]. They showed that for independent log-concave random vectors, under linear volume preserving maps, inequality (1.1) can be reversed at the cost of a constant factor on the r.h.s of the inequality. This can be thought of as a functional analog of Milman’s reverse BMI for convex bodies [13]. It is necessary to place log-concave random vectors “at right positions” via linear volume preserving maps for the reversed EPI to hold. We are interested in the sharp reverse EPI for independent and identically distributed (or i.i.d. for short) log-concave random vectors. In this case, linear volume preserving maps are not needed and the question can be phrased as follows.

Conjecture 1.1 (Folklore).

Let XX and YY be i.i.d. log-concave random vectors taking values in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The entropy increment h⁡(X+Y)−h⁡(X)h(X+Y)-h(X) is maximized when XX and YY have exponential distributions.

Clearly, the entropy increment is affine invariant. An earlier result of Cover and Zhang [6] shows that log-concavity and identical distribution (without independence between XX and YY) yield the upper bound d​log⁡2d\log 2 of the entropy increment. Huang, Slomka, Tkocz, and Vritsiou ([10], Section 6) observed that the improvement of Cover and Zhang’s bound for Conjecture 1.1 will lead to important progress on Hadwiger’s covering problem. Ball, Nayar, and Tkocz [2] studied the entropy increment for a two dimensional log-concave random vector (X,Y)(X,Y), whose marginals have identical differential entropy (but not necessarily independent). This variant of reverse EPI and its generalizations are entropic analogs of Busemann’s convexity theorem of intersection bodies [4] and the convexity of pp-cross-section bodies conjectured by Gardner and Giannopoulos [8] (the end of Section 5, and the discussion in [11]).

Aforementioned forward and reverse EPIs have been studied for general Rényi entropies. For p∈(0,1)∪(1,∞)p\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty), the order pp Rényi entropy of XX is defined as

hp​(X)=11−p​log​∫ℝdf​(x)p​𝑑x.h_{p}(X)=\frac{1}{1-p}\log\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x)^{p}dx. (1.2)

For p∈{0,1,∞}p\in\{0,1,\infty\}, by taking limits, we have h0​(X)=log⁡|supp⁡{f}|h_{0}(X)=\log|\mathrm{supp}\{f\}|, h∞​(X)=−log⁡‖f‖∞h_{\infty}(X)=-\log\|f\|_{\infty}, and h1(X)=h(X)=−∫ℝdf(x)logf(x)dxh_{1}(X)=h(X)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x)\log f(x)dx. Here, we denote by |supp​{f}||\mathrm{supp}\{f\}| the Lebesgue measure of the support of ff, and ‖f‖∞\|f\|_{\infty} is the essential supremum of ff, and h1​(X)h_{1}(X) is the classical differential entropy h⁡(X)h(X) of XX.

It is suspected that a transition will occur in the increment of Rényi entropy. More precisely, there exists an absolute constant p0∈(0,1)p_{0}\in(0,1) such that hp​(X+Y)−hp​(X)h_{p}(X+Y)-h_{p}(X) is maximized by exponential random vectors for p≥p0p\geq p_{0}, and is maximized by uniform random vectors taking values in the cube [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} for 0<p≤p00<p\leq p_{0}. It is perhaps worth to point out that the increment of Rényi entropy of order p>1p>1 (respectively, 0<p<10<p<1) boils down to the minimization (respectively, maximization) of ‖f∗f‖p/‖f‖p\|f\ast f\|_{p}/\|f\|_{p} over the class of integrable log-concave functions. This can be thought of as a special type of reverse Young’s convolution inequality. Our main result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.2.

Let XX and YY be independent real-valued log-concave random variables. Let ZZ and WW be independent exponential random variables such that h∞​(Z)=h∞​(X)h_{\infty}(Z)=h_{\infty}(X) and h∞​(W)=h∞​(Y)h_{\infty}(W)=h_{\infty}(Y). We have

h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(Z+W).\displaystyle h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(Z+W).

A discrete analog holds for integer-valued monotone log-concave random variables.

Remark 1.3.

If X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n} are independent real-valued random variables, and U1,⋯,UnU_{1},\cdots,U_{n} are independent uniform random variables such that h∞​(Ui)=h∞​(Xi)h_{\infty}(U_{i})=h_{\infty}(X_{i}) for i=1,⋯,ni=1,\cdots,n, Rogozin [17] proved that

h∞​(X1+⋯+Xn)≥h∞​(U1+⋯+Un).h_{\infty}(X_{1}+\cdots+X_{n})\geq h_{\infty}(U_{1}+\cdots+U_{n}).

Hence, our result can also be seen as a reverse Rogozin type result for two log-concave random variables. However, we are not able to establish analogs of Theorem 1.2 for three or more log-concave random variables or in multi-dimensions.

Another related problem is the characterization of log-concave distributions that maximize the Rényi entropic increment hp​(X−Y)−hp​(X)h_{p}(X-Y)-h_{p}(X). In this case, it is suspected that exponential distributions are always maximizers. This resembles the Rogers-Shephard inequality in convex geometry [16]. In a certain sense, the symmetry of X−YX-Y (implicitly) makes this problem more tractable than its counterpart of the X+YX+Y case. Melbourne and Tkocz ([15], Theorem VI.1) showed that the increment of Rényi entropy of order p≥2p\geq 2 is indeed maximized by exponential random vectors. A discrete analog was obtained by Melbourne and Palafox-Castillo ([14], Theorem 2.11) for integer-valued monotone log-concave random variables.

2. Rearrangement and majorization

Rearrangement and majorization are classical tools for establishing sharp geometric and functional inequalities. This section provides the necessary preliminaries on decreasing rearrangement and majorization theory in one dimension. Readers already familiar with rearrangement theory are encouraged to skip this section.

2.1. Decreasing rearrangement

Let A⊆ℝA\subseteq\mathbb{R} be a Borel measurable set with Lebesgue measure |A||A|. The decreasing rearrangement of AA is defined as A↓=[0,|A|)A^{\downarrow}=[0,|A|). The following properties of decreasing rearrangement may be scattered in the literature. We provide proof of them for the convenience of the reader.

Proposition 2.1.

Let A,B⊆ℝA,B\subseteq\mathbb{R} be Borel measurable sets.

  1. (1)

    For all λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, it holds that (λ​A)↓=λ​A↓(\lambda A)^{\downarrow}=\lambda A^{\downarrow}.

  2. (2)

    It holds that A↓+B↓⊆(A+B)↓A^{\downarrow}+B^{\downarrow}\subseteq(A+B)^{\downarrow}.

  3. (3)

    Let {An}n=1∞\{A_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} be a sequence of measurable sets such that An⊆An+1A_{n}\subseteq A_{n+1} for all n=1,2⋯n=1,2\cdots. It holds that (∪n=1∞An)↓=∪n=1∞An↓(\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n})^{\downarrow}=\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}^{\downarrow}.

Proof.

Statement (1) readily follows from the definition. By definition, A↓=[0,|A|)A^{\downarrow}=[0,|A|), B↓=[0,|B|)B^{\downarrow}=[0,|B|), and (A+B)↓=[0,|A+B|)(A+B)^{\downarrow}=[0,|A+B|). The Brunn-Minkowski inequality in one dimension yields |A+B|≥|A|+|B||A+B|\geq|A|+|B|. Hence, A↓+B↓=[0,|A|+|B|)⊆(A+B)↓A^{\downarrow}+B^{\downarrow}=[0,|A|+|B|)\subseteq(A+B)^{\downarrow}. This proves statement (2).

By definition, An↓=[0,|An|)A_{n}^{\downarrow}=[0,|A_{n}|). Since An⊆An+1A_{n}\subseteq A_{n+1}, we have

∪n=1∞An↓=[0,limn→∞|An|)=[0,|∪n=1∞An|)=(∪n=1∞An)↓.\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}^{\downarrow}=\big[0,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}|A_{n}|\big)=\left[0,|\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n}|\right)=(\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_{n})^{\downarrow}.

This proves the last statement. ∎

Let f:ℝ→ℝ∪{±∞}f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\} be a Borel measurable function such that all super level sets {f>λ}\{f>\lambda\} have finite measures (which is called vanishing at infinity). We define the decreasing rearrangement f↓:ℝ+→ℝ∪{±∞}f^{\downarrow}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\} as

f↓(x)=sup{λ∈ℝ:x∈{f>λ}↓}.f^{\downarrow}(x)=\sup\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:x\in\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}\right\}. (2.1)
Proposition 2.2.

Let f:ℝ→ℝ∪{±∞}f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\} be a Borel measurable function.

  1. (1)

    For all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, it holds that {f↓>λ}={f>λ}↓\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda\}=\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}. (Hence, this gives an equivalent definition of the decreasing rearrangement f↓f^{\downarrow}).

  2. (2)

    If ff is concave, then f↓f^{\downarrow} is also concave. Consequently, if ff is log-concave, then f↓f^{\downarrow} is also log-concave.

Proof.

For each x∈{f↓>λ}x\in\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda\}, by the definition of f↓f^{\downarrow} in (2.1), there exists λx>λ\lambda_{x}>\lambda such that x∈{f>λx}↓⊆{f>λ}↓x\in\{f>\lambda_{x}\}^{\downarrow}\subseteq\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}. This shows that {f↓>λ}⊆{f>λ}↓\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda\}\subseteq\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}. To see the other direction, we apply Proposition 2.1 (statement (3)) to write

{f>λ}↓=(∪n=1∞{f>λ+1/n})↓=∪n=1∞{f>λ+1/n}↓.\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}=\left(\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{f>\lambda+1/n\}\right)^{\downarrow}=\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{f>\lambda+1/n\}^{\downarrow}.

Hence, for each x∈{f>λ}↓x\in\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}, there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that x∈{f>λ+1/n}↓x\in\{f>\lambda+1/n\}^{\downarrow}. By the definition of f↓f^{\downarrow} in (2.1), this yields f↓​(x)≥λ+1/n>λf^{\downarrow}(x)\geq\lambda+1/n>\lambda, and hence, x∈{f↓>λ}x\in\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda\}. This completes the proof of the first statement.

Suppose ff is concave. This is equivalent to the following set-theoretic inequality. For any λ0,λ1∈ℝ\lambda_{0},\lambda_{1}\in\mathbb{R} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], it holds that

(1−t){f>λ0}+t{f>λ1}⊆{f>(1−t)λ0+tλ1}.(1-t)\{f>\lambda_{0}\}+t\{f>\lambda_{1}\}\subseteq\{f>(1-t)\lambda_{0}+t\lambda_{1}\}. (2.2)

Next we prove the inclusion inequality (2.2) for f↓f^{\downarrow}. This will yield the concavity of f↓f^{\downarrow}. We apply statement (1) of the current proposition and Proposition 2.1 (statements (1) and (2)) to obtain

(1−t){f↓>λ0}+t{f↓>λ1}\displaystyle(1-t)\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda_{0}\}+t\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda_{1}\} =(1−t){f>λ0}↓+t{f>λ1}↓\displaystyle=(1-t)\{f>\lambda_{0}\}^{\downarrow}+t\{f>\lambda_{1}\}^{\downarrow}
=((1−t){f>λ0})↓+(t{f>λ1})↓\displaystyle=((1-t)\{f>\lambda_{0}\})^{\downarrow}+(t\{f>\lambda_{1}\})^{\downarrow}
⊆((1−t){f>λ0}+t{f>λ1})↓\displaystyle\subseteq((1-t)\{f>\lambda_{0}\}+t\{f>\lambda_{1}\})^{\downarrow}
⊆{f>(1−t)λ0+tλ1}↓\displaystyle\subseteq\{f>(1-t)\lambda_{0}+t\lambda_{1}\}^{\downarrow}
={f↓>(1−t)λ0+tλ1}.\displaystyle=\{f^{\downarrow}>(1-t)\lambda_{0}+t\lambda_{1}\}.

Suppose f⁡(x)=eV⁡(x)f(x)=e^{V(x)} is log-concave, i.e., V⁡(x)V(x) is concave. Write f↓​(x)=eV~​(x)f^{\downarrow}(x)=e^{\tilde{V}(x)}. For all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, we have

{V~>λ}={f↓>eλ}={f>eλ}↓={V>λ}↓.\{\tilde{V}>\lambda\}=\{f^{\downarrow}>e^{\lambda}\}=\{f>e^{\lambda}\}^{\downarrow}=\{V>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}.

Using the first statement, we conclude that V~=V↓\tilde{V}=V^{\downarrow}. Since VV is concave, V↓V^{\downarrow}, and hence, V~\tilde{V} are concave. (One can show the concavity of V~\tilde{V} by establishing the corresponding set-theoretic inequality). This yields the log-concavity of f↓f^{\downarrow}. ∎

The following is a reverse Hardy-Littlewood type inequality.

Lemma 2.3.

Let f,gf,g be non-negative functions supported on [a,b][a,b]. Then it holds

∫abf⁡(x)​g​(x)​𝑑x≥∫0b−af↓​(x)​g↓​(b−a−x)​𝑑x.\int_{a}^{b}f(x)g(x)dx\geq\int_{0}^{b-a}f^{\downarrow}(x)g^{\downarrow}(b-a-x)dx.
Proof.

Write f⁡(x)=∫0f⁡(x)𝑑λf(x)=\int_{0}^{f(x)}d\lambda, g⁡(x)=∫0g⁡(x)𝑑σg(x)=\int_{0}^{g(x)}d\sigma and apply Fubini-Tonelli’s theorem to obtain

∫abf⁡(x)​g​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)g(x)dx =∫0∞∫0∞∫ab𝟙{f>λ}(x)𝟙{g>σ}(x)dxdλdσ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{a}^{b}\mathbbm{1}_{\{f>\lambda\}}(x)\mathbbm{1}_{\{g>\sigma\}}(x)dxd\lambda d\sigma
=∫0∞∫0∞|{f>λ}∩{g>σ}|dλdσ.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}|\{f>\lambda\}\cap\{g>\sigma\}|d\lambda d\sigma.

Similarly, we have

∫0b−af↓​(x)​g↓​(b−a−x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{0}^{b-a}f^{\downarrow}(x)g^{\downarrow}(b-a-x)dx =∫0∞∫0∞|{f↓>λ}∩(b−a−{g↓>σ})|dλdσ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}|\{f^{\downarrow}>\lambda\}\cap(b-a-\{g^{\downarrow}>\sigma\})|d\lambda d\sigma
=∫0∞∫0∞|{f>λ}↓∩(b−a−{g>σ}↓)|dλdσ,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}|\{f>\lambda\}^{\downarrow}\cap(b-a-\{g>\sigma\}^{\downarrow})|d\lambda d\sigma,

where the second equality follows from Proposition 2.2 (statement (1)). Then the statement can be proved by applying the following inequality to A={f>λ},B={g>σ}A=\{f>\lambda\},B=\{g>\sigma\}. For any measurable sets A,B⊆[a,b]A,B\subseteq[a,b], it holds that

|A↓∩(b−a−B↓)|≤|A∩B|.|A^{\downarrow}\cap(b-a-B^{\downarrow})|\leq|A\cap B|.

We assume that A↓∩(b−a−B↓)≠∅A^{\downarrow}\cap(b-a-B^{\downarrow})\neq\emptyset. Note A↓=[0,|A|)A^{\downarrow}=[0,|A|) and b−a−B↓=[b−a−|B|,b−a)b-a-B^{\downarrow}=[b-a-|B|,b-a). Hence, we have

|A↓∩(b−a−B↓)|\displaystyle|A^{\downarrow}\cap(b-a-B^{\downarrow})| =|A|−(b−a−|B|)\displaystyle=|A|-(b-a-|B|)
=|A|+|B|−(b−a)\displaystyle=|A|+|B|-(b-a)
≤|A|+|B|−|A∪B|\displaystyle\leq|A|+|B|-|A\cup B|
=|A∩B|.\displaystyle=|A\cap B|.

This completes the proof. ∎

2.2. Majorization

Let f,g:ℝ→ℝ+f,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} be two integrable functions such that

∫ℝf⁡(x)​𝑑x=∫ℝg⁡(x)​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)dx{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}.}

We say that ff is majorized by gg if it holds for all t≥0t\geq 0 that

∫ℝ(f⁡(x)−t)+​𝑑x≤∫ℝ(g⁡(x)−t)+​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}(f(x)-t)_{+}dx\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g(x)-t)_{+}dx. (2.3)

For t≥0t\geq 0, we write mf​(t)=|{x∈ℝ:f⁡(x)>t}|m_{f}(t)=|\{x\in\mathbb{R}:f(x)>t\}| and define mg​(t)m_{g}(t) in a similar manner. Then we can rewrite (2.3) as

∫t∞mf​(s)​𝑑s≤∫t∞mg​(s)​𝑑s.\int_{t}^{\infty}m_{f}(s)ds\leq\int_{t}^{\infty}m_{g}(s)ds.

A real-valued function ff on ℝ\mathbb{R} is called unimodal if there exists a point x0x_{0} such that ff is non-decreasing for x<x0x<x_{0} and non-increasing for x>x0x>x_{0}. Clearly, log-concave functions are unimodal. The following result provides a sufficient condition for the majorization of gg over ff.

Proposition 2.4.

Suppose that for any Borel measurable set AA of finite measure, there exists a Borel measurable set BB with equal measure as AA such that

∫Af⁡(x)​𝑑x≤∫Bg⁡(x)​𝑑x.\int_{A}f(x)dx\leq\int_{B}g(x)dx. (2.4)

Then ff is majorized by gg. If ff and gg are unimodal, it suffices to verify the above inequality for intervals.

Proof.

For any given t∈ℝ+t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, we write A={f>t}A=\{f>t\}. Then there exists B⊆ℝB\subseteq\mathbb{R} of the same measure as AA such that

∫ℝ(f⁡(x)−t)+​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}(f(x)-t)_{+}dx =∫A(f⁡(x)−t)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{A}(f(x)-t)dx
≤∫B(g⁡(x)−t)​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq\int_{B}(g(x)-t)dx
≤∫B(g⁡(x)−t)+​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq\int_{B}(g(x)-t)_{+}dx
≤∫ℝ(g⁡(x)−t)+​𝑑x.\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g(x)-t)_{+}dx.

This shows the majorization of gg over ff.

Note that the integral of a unimodal function over all measurable sets of fixed measure attains its maximum for an interval. Therefore, if ff is unimodal, it is sufficient to evaluate the integral on the left-hand side of inequality (2.4) over intervals. Moreover, when gg is also unimodal, one often considers the integral on the right-hand side of inequality (2.4) over intervals, even though considering general Borel measurable sets with the same measure as AA would suffice. ∎

he following characterization of the majorization relation is well known. A preliminary version was first proved by Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya [9] and various extensions were discussed in Chong [5]. For the proof, we refer the reader to Theorem 2.1 in [5] and Theorem 15.27 in [19]; a related result can also be found in Proposition 7.3 of [21].

Proposition 2.5.

Let ff and gg be non-negative functions on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Then ff is majorized by gg if and only if for all non-negative increasing convex functions ϕ:ℝ+→ℝ+\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} with ϕ⁡(0)=0\phi(0)=0 it holds that

∫ℝϕ⁡(f⁡(x))​𝑑x≤∫ℝϕ⁡(g⁡(x))​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(f(x))dx\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi(g(x))dx. (2.5)

3. Main Results

Proposition 3.1.

Let XX and YY be i.i.d. log-concave random vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We have

h2​(X+Y)≤h2​(X)+d​log⁡2.h_{2}(X+Y)\leq h_{2}(X)+d\log 2. (3.1)

Moreover, the inequality can not be improved.

Remark 3.2.

One can check that equality of (3.1) can be achieved by exponential and Laplace distributions with densities ∏i=1dλi​e−λi​xi​𝟙ℝ+​(xi)\prod_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{i}e^{-\lambda_{i}x_{i}}\mathbbm{1}_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(x_{i}), and ∏i=1dλi2​e−λi​|xi|\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{2}e^{-\lambda_{i}|x_{i}|}, respectively, where λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 for i=1,⋯,di=1,\cdots,d.

Proof.

Let X~\tilde{X} and Y~\tilde{Y} be independent copies of XX and YY, respectively. Let ff be the density of X−X~X-\tilde{X}. Since ff is symmetric and log-concave, we have

‖f∗f‖∞=(f∗f)​(0)=∫ℝdf​(x)2​𝑑x≥f⁡(0)​∫ℝdf⁡(2​x)​𝑑x=f⁡(0)2d.\|f\ast f\|_{\infty}=(f\ast f)(0)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(x)^{2}dx\geq f(0)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(2x)dx=\frac{f(0)}{2^{d}}.

This can be rewritten as

h∞​((X−X~)+(Y−Y~))≤h∞​(X−X~)+d​log⁡2.h_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})+(Y-\tilde{Y}))\leq h_{\infty}(X-\tilde{X})+d\log 2.

For any i.i.d. log-concave random vectors UU and VV, it holds that h∞​(U−V)=h2​(U)h_{\infty}(U-V)=h_{2}(U). This observation, together with the inequality above, implies that

h2​(X+Y)\displaystyle h_{2}(X+Y) =h∞​((X+Y)−(X~+Y~))\displaystyle=h_{\infty}((X+Y)-(\tilde{X}+\tilde{Y}))
=h∞​((X−X~)+(Y−Y~))\displaystyle=h_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})+(Y-\tilde{Y})) (3.2)
≤h∞​(X−X~)+d​log⁡2\displaystyle\leq h_{\infty}(X-\tilde{X})+d\log 2
=h2​(X)+d​log⁡2.\displaystyle=h_{2}(X)+d\log 2.

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark 3.3.

Note that X−X~X-\tilde{X} and Y−Y~Y-\tilde{Y} are symmetric and independent. Then, we can proceed with (3.2) to obtain

h2​(X+Y)\displaystyle h_{2}(X+Y) =h∞​((X−X~)+(Y−Y~))\displaystyle=h_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})+(Y-\tilde{Y}))
=h∞​((X−X~)−(Y−Y~))\displaystyle=h_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})-(Y-\tilde{Y}))
=h∞​((X−Y)−(X~−Y~))\displaystyle=h_{\infty}((X-Y)-(\tilde{X}-\tilde{Y}))
=h2​(X−Y).\displaystyle=h_{2}(X-Y).

Hence, inequality (3.1) is the same as the p=2p=2 case of Theorem VI.1 of Melbourne and Tkocz [15]. For any log-concave random vector (X,Y)∈ℝ2(X,Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, it was proved in [11] that

eh2​(X+Y)≤eh2​(X)+eh2​(Y),e^{h_{2}(X+Y)}\leq e^{h_{2}(X)}+e^{h_{2}(Y)},

which implies the one-dimensional case of (3.1) as long as X,YX,Y are jointly log-concave (even not necessarily independent) and have equal entropy h2​(X)=h2​(Y)h_{2}(X)=h_{2}(Y).

Theorem 3.4.

Let XX and YY be independent real-valued log-concave random variables. Let ZZ and WW be independent exponential random variables such that h∞​(Z)=h∞​(X)h_{\infty}(Z)=h_{\infty}(X) and h∞​(W)=h∞​(Y)h_{\infty}(W)=h_{\infty}(Y). We have

h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(Z+W).\displaystyle h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(Z+W). (3.3)

Consequently, for i.i.d. real-valued log-concave random variables XX and YY, we have

h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(X)+1.\displaystyle h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(X)+1. (3.4)

The decreasing rearrangement operation tends to increase concentration on one side while reducing the additive overlap of translates in the convolution. Consequently, one expects f↓∗f↓f^{\downarrow}\ast f^{\downarrow} to be less concentrated than f∗ff\ast f. This behavior is illustrated by the following result, which can be viewed as a reverse of Riesz’s rearrangement inequality. The proof draws from our communication with James Melbourne.

Lemma 3.5.

Let f,g:ℝ→ℝ+f,g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} be integrable unimodal functions. Then it holds that

‖f∗g‖∞≥‖f↓∗g↓‖∞.\|f\ast g\|_{\infty}\geq\|f^{\downarrow}\ast g^{\downarrow}\|_{\infty}.
Proof.

For any given z≥0z\geq 0, the unimodality of ff and gg implies that there exist two intervals A=[α,α+z]A=[\alpha,\alpha+z] and B=[β,β+z]B=[\beta,\beta+z] such that

(fA)↓​(y)=f↓​(y),(gB)↓​(y)=g↓​(y),for all​y∈[0,z].(f_{A})^{\downarrow}(y)=f^{\downarrow}(y),\quad(g_{B})^{\downarrow}(y)=g^{\downarrow}(y),\quad\text{for all}~y\in[0,z].

(Here, we write fEf_{E} and gEg_{E} for the restrictions of ff and gg to E⊆ℝE\subseteq\mathbb{R}, respectively). For y∈Ay\in A, we define g~​(y)=gB​(γz−y)\tilde{g}(y)=g_{B}(\gamma_{z}-y), where γz=α+β+z\gamma_{z}=\alpha+\beta+z, so that both g~\tilde{g} and fAf_{A} are supported on AA.. Note that reflection and translation preserve the decreasing rearrangement of a function. Thus we have

(g~)↓​(y)=(gB)↓​(y),for all​y∈[0,z].(\tilde{g})^{\downarrow}(y)=(g_{B})^{\downarrow}(y),\quad\text{for all}~y\in[0,z].

Now we apply Lemma 2.3 to obtain

(f↓∗g↓)​(z)\displaystyle(f^{\downarrow}\ast g^{\downarrow})(z) =∫0zf↓​(y)​g↓​(z−y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{z}f^{\downarrow}(y)g^{\downarrow}(z-y)dy
=∫0z(fA)↓​(y)​(gB)↓​(z−y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{z}(f_{A})^{\downarrow}(y)(g_{B})^{\downarrow}(z-y)dy
=∫0z(fA)↓​(y)​(g~)↓​(z−y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{z}(f_{A})^{\downarrow}(y)(\tilde{g})^{\downarrow}(z-y)dy
≤∫αα+zfA​(y)​g~​(y)​𝑑y\displaystyle\leq\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+z}f_{A}(y)\tilde{g}(y)dy
=∫αα+zfA​(y)​gB​(γz−y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+z}f_{A}(y)g_{B}(\gamma_{z}-y)dy
=∫αα+zf⁡(y)​g​(γz−y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{\alpha}^{\alpha+z}f(y)g(\gamma_{z}-y)dy
≤(f∗g)​(γz).\displaystyle\leq(f\ast g)(\gamma_{z}).

Then we can obtain the result by taking the supremum over z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}. ∎

Remark 3.6.

As shown in the proof, unimodality guarantees the existence of intervals AA and BB such that (fA)↓=f↓(f_{A})^{\downarrow}=f^{\downarrow} and (gB)↓=g↓(g_{B})^{\downarrow}=g^{\downarrow} on [0,z][0,z]. The result may fail for arbitrary functions that lack this interval structure. For example, define f=𝟏[0,2]f=\mathbf{1}_{[0,2]} and g=𝟏[0,1]+𝟏[3,4]g=\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}+\mathbf{1}_{[3,4]}. Clearly, f↓=g↓=𝟏[0,2]f^{\downarrow}=g^{\downarrow}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,2]}. One can check that ‖f∗g‖∞=1\|f\ast g\|_{\infty}=1 while ‖f↓∗g↓‖∞=2\|f^{\downarrow}\ast g^{\downarrow}\|_{\infty}=2.

Lemma 3.7.

Let XX and YY be independent monotone log-concave random variables. Let ZZ and WW be independent exponential random variables such that h∞​(Z)=h∞​(X)h_{\infty}(Z)=h_{\infty}(X) and h∞​(W)=h∞​(Y)h_{\infty}(W)=h_{\infty}(Y). For all 0<p≤∞0<p\leq\infty, we have

hp​(X+Y)≤hp​(Z+W).\displaystyle h_{p}(X+Y)\leq h_{p}(Z+W). (3.5)
Proof.

We will show the majorization of X+YX+Y over X+WX+W (i.e., the density of X+YX+Y majorizes that of X+WX+W) and, in the same vein, the majorization of X+WX+W over Z+WZ+W. Hence, Z+WZ+W is majorized by X+YX+Y. This, together with inequality (2.5), yields the statement (3.5).

Now, we show the majorization of X+YX+Y over X+WX+W. Note that X+YX+Y and X+WX+W are log-concave. By Proposition 2.4, it suffice to show that for any [a,a+δ]⊆[0,∞)[a,a+\delta]\subseteq[0,\infty), there exists [b,b+δ]⊆[0,∞)[b,b+\delta]\subseteq[0,\infty) such that

ℙ⁡(X+W∈[a,a+δ])≤ℙ⁡(X+Y∈[b,b+δ]).{\mathbb{P}}(X+W\in[a,a+\delta])\leq{\mathbb{P}}(X+Y\in[b,b+\delta]). (3.6)

Let fXf_{X} and fYf_{Y} be the densities of XX and YY, respectively. We can perturb fXf_{X} and fYf_{Y} if necessary such that both of them have infinite support. We can also make shifts if necessary so that ‖fX‖∞=fX​(0)\|f_{X}\|_{\infty}=f_{X}(0) and ‖fY‖∞=fY​(0)\|f_{Y}\|_{\infty}=f_{Y}(0). Write fY​(x)=fY​(0)​e−V⁡(x)f_{Y}(x)=f_{Y}(0)e^{-V(x)} for x≥0x\geq 0, where V⁡(x)V(x) is an non-decreasing convex function with V⁡(0)=0V(0)=0. Then WW has density fW​(x)=fY​(0)​e−fY​(0)​xf_{W}(x)=f_{Y}(0)e^{-f_{Y}(0)x} for x≥0x\geq 0. Consider the map ϕ=FW−1∘FY\phi=F_{W}^{-1}\circ F_{Y}, where FYF_{Y} and FWF_{W} are the cumulative distribution functions of YY and WW, respectively. One can check that W​=𝑑​ϕ​(Y)W\overset{d}{=}\phi(Y) and ϕ⁡(y)=−fY​(0)−1​log⁡(1−FY​(y))\phi(y)=-f_{Y}(0)^{-1}\log(1-F_{Y}(y)). Then we can rewrite inequality (3.6) as

ℙ⁡(X+ϕ⁡(Y)∈[a,a+δ])≤ℙ⁡(X+Y∈[b,b+δ]).{\mathbb{P}}(X+\phi(Y)\in[a,a+\delta])\leq{\mathbb{P}}(X+Y\in[b,b+\delta]).

By conditioning on YY, it suffices to show for all y≥0y\geq 0 that

ℙ⁡(X∈[a,a+δ]−ϕ⁡(y))≤ℙ⁡(X∈[b,b+δ]−y).\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}(X\in[a,a+\delta]-\phi(y))\leq{\mathbb{P}}(X\in[b,b+\delta]-y). (3.7)

Next, we demonstrate that this inequality holds for b=ϕ−1​(a)b=\phi^{-1}(a). Since YY is log-concave, the tail probability 1−FY​(y)1-F_{Y}(y) is also log-concave. Hence, ϕ\phi is a convex map. Furthermore, we have

ϕ′​(y)=e−V⁡(y)1−FY​(y).\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}(y)=\frac{e^{-V(y)}}{1-F_{Y}(y)}. (3.8)

Since ϕ\phi is convex, ϕ′\phi^{\prime} is nondecreasing, thus ϕ′​(y)≥ϕ′​(0)=1\phi^{\prime}(y)\geq\phi^{\prime}(0)=1.

Case 1: y≥ϕ−1​(a+δ)y\geq\phi^{-1}(a+\delta). Since XX is non-negative, inequality (3.7) trivially holds.

Case 2: ϕ−1​(a)<y<ϕ−1​(a+δ)\phi^{-1}(a)<y<\phi^{-1}(a+\delta). By integrating ϕ′\phi^{\prime} over [ϕ−1​(a),y][\phi^{-1}(a),y], ϕ′≥1\phi^{\prime}\geq 1 implies that y−ϕ−1​(a)≤ϕ⁡(y)−ay-\phi^{-1}(a)\leq\phi(y)-a, which is equivalent to a+δ−ϕ⁡(y)≤ϕ−1​(a)+δ−ya+\delta-\phi(y)\leq\phi^{-1}(a)+\delta-y. Since XX is non-negative, we obtain

ℙ⁡(X∈[0,a+δ−ϕ⁡(y)]≤ℙ⁡(X∈[0,ϕ−1​(a)+δ−y])CLOSE,{\mathbb{P}}(X\in[0,a+\delta-\phi(y)]\leq{\mathbb{P}}(X\in[0,\phi^{-1}(a)+\delta-y]),

which is inequality (3.7).

Case 3: y≤ϕ−1​(a)y\leq\phi^{-1}(a). Similar to Case 2, we can apply ϕ′≥1\phi^{\prime}\geq 1 to obtain a−ϕ⁡(y)≥ϕ−1​(a)−y≥0a-\phi(y)\geq\phi^{-1}(a)-y\geq 0 by integrating ϕ′\phi^{\prime} over [y,ϕ−1​(a)][y,\phi^{-1}(a)]. This, together with the monotonicity of the density of XX, yields inequality (3.7). ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Let fXf_{X} and fYf_{Y} be the densities of log-concave random variables XX and YY, respectively. As shown in Proposition 2.2, log-concavity is preserved by decreasing rearrangement, thus fX↓f_{X}^{\downarrow} and fY↓f_{Y}^{\downarrow} are also log-concave. Since decreasing rearrangement preserves the LpL^{p} moments, fX↓f_{X}^{\downarrow} and fY↓f_{Y}^{\downarrow} are also probability densities such that ‖fX↓‖∞=‖fX‖∞\|f_{X}^{\downarrow}\|_{\infty}=\|f_{X}\|_{\infty} and ‖fY↓‖∞=‖fY‖∞\|f_{Y}^{\downarrow}\|_{\infty}=\|f_{Y}\|_{\infty}. Let X↓X^{\downarrow} and Y↓Y^{\downarrow} be random variables with densities fX↓f_{X}^{\downarrow} and fY↓f_{Y}^{\downarrow}, respectively. Then we have

h∞​(X↓)=h∞​(X)=h∞​(Z),h∞​(Y↓)=h∞​(Y)=h∞​(W).h_{\infty}(X^{\downarrow})=h_{\infty}(X)=h_{\infty}(Z),~~~~h_{\infty}(Y^{\downarrow})=h_{\infty}(Y)=h_{\infty}(W).

By Lemma 3.5, we have

h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(X↓+Y↓).h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(X^{\downarrow}+Y^{\downarrow}).

By Lemma 3.7, we have

h∞​(X↓+Y↓)≤h∞​(Z+W).h_{\infty}(X^{\downarrow}+Y^{\downarrow})\leq h_{\infty}(Z+W).

Then we can combine these inequalities to obtain inequality (3.3). Inequality (3.4) follows from simple calculations. ∎

Remark 3.8.

We give a short proof of the p=∞p=\infty case of inequality (3.5) via measure transportation (in fact the change of variable). (This, together with Lemma 3.5, yields a short proof of Theorem 3.4). Since the map ϕ\phi transports YY to WW, it holds for any function φ\varphi integrable with respect to FWF_{W} that

∫ℝ+φ⁡(ϕ⁡(x))​fY​(x)​𝑑x=∫ℝ+φ⁡(x)​fW​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\varphi(\phi(x))f_{Y}(x)dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\varphi(x)f_{W}(x)dx.

For any y≥0y\geq 0, we apply this identity to φ⁡(x)=fX​(y−x)\varphi(x)=f_{X}(y-x) for 0≤x≤y0\leq x\leq y to obtain

(fX∗fW)​(y)\displaystyle(f_{X}\ast f_{W})(y) =∫0yfX​(y−x)​fW​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{y}f_{X}(y-x)f_{W}(x)dx
=∫0ϕ−1​(y)fX​(y−ϕ⁡(x))​fY​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\phi^{-1}(y)}f_{X}(y-\phi(x))f_{Y}(x)dx
≤∫0ϕ−1​(y)fX​(ϕ−1​(y)−x)​fY​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\phi^{-1}(y)}f_{X}(\phi^{-1}(y)-x)f_{Y}(x)dx
=(fX∗fY)​(ϕ−1​(y)),\displaystyle=(f_{X}\ast f_{Y})(\phi^{-1}(y)),

where the inequality follows from the observation that y−ϕ⁡(x)≥ϕ−1​(y)−xy-\phi(x)\geq\phi^{-1}(y)-x, which is implied by (3.8), and the assumption that fXf_{X} is non-increasing. This yields

h∞​(X+Y)≤h∞​(X+W)h_{\infty}(X+Y)\leq h_{\infty}(X+W)

and similarly we can obtain

h∞​(X+W)≤h∞​(Z+W).h_{\infty}(X+W)\leq h_{\infty}(Z+W).

These two inequalities together yield the p=∞p=\infty case of inequality (3.5). One can see that the monotonicity of fXf_{X} and the expansion property of the transportation map ϕ\phi play the key role.

Remark 3.9.

Let (X,Y)(X,Y) be an origin symmetric log-concave random vector in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. (The marginals are not necessarily independent). A result of Ball ([1], Theorem 5) imply that

eh∞​(X+Y)≤eh∞​(X)+eh∞​(Y).e^{h_{\infty}(X+Y)}\leq e^{h_{\infty}(X)}+e^{h_{\infty}(Y)}.

This inequality can be seen as the entropic analog of Busemann’s convexity theorem of intersection bodies [4], which also motivates the study of reverse EPIs in [2, 11].

4. Analogs for Interger-valued Log-concave Random Variables

We first recall the majorization of two sequences. Let {f⁡(k)}k=1∞\{f(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} and {g⁡(k)}k=1∞\{g(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} be two summable non-negative sequences such that ∑k=1∞f⁡(k)=∑k=1∞g⁡(k)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f(k)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}g(k). We say that {f⁡(k)}k=1∞\{f(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} majorizes {g⁡(k)}k=1∞\{g(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} if the decreasing rearrangements {f↓​(k)}k=1∞\{f^{\downarrow}(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} and {g↓​(k)}k=1∞\{g^{\downarrow}(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} satisfy that ∑k=1nf↓​(k)≥∑k=1kg↓​(k)\sum_{k=1}^{n}f^{\downarrow}(k)\geq\sum_{k=1}^{k}g^{\downarrow}(k) for all n∈ℤ+n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Karamata’s inequality (or majorization inequality) says that if {f⁡(k)}k=1∞\{f(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} majorizes {g⁡(k)}k=1∞\{g(k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty} then it holds for any convex function φ\varphi on ℝ\mathbb{R} that

∑k=1∞(φ∘f)​(k)≥∑k=1∞(φ∘g)​(k).\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\varphi\circ f)(k)\geq\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\varphi\circ g)(k). (4.1)

An integer-valued random variable XX is called log-concave if its probability mass function {f⁡(k)}k∈ℤ\{f(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} is a log-concave sequence; that is, f​(k+1)2≥f⁡(k)​f​(k+2)f(k+1)^{2}\geq f(k)f(k+2) holds for all k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} and the support of this sequence is a contiguous interval of ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Similar to (1.2), the order pp Rényi entropy of XX is defined as

Hp​(X)=11−p​log​∑k∈ℤf​(k)p.H_{p}(X)=\frac{1}{1-p}\log\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)^{p}.

Particularly, we have H∞​(X)=−log⁡‖f‖∞H_{\infty}(X)=-\log\|f\|_{\infty}.

Proposition 4.1.

Let XX and YY be i.i.d log-concave random variables on ℤ\mathbb{Z}. It holds that

H2​(X+Y)<H2​(X)+log⁡2.H_{2}(X+Y)<H_{2}(X)+\log 2. (4.2)

Moreover, the inequality cannot be improved.

Proof.

Let X~\tilde{X} and Y~\tilde{Y} be independent copies of XX and YY, respectively. We denote by {f⁡(k)}k∈ℤ\{f(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} the probability mass function of X−X~X-\tilde{X}. We define the geometric sequence {g⁡(k)}k∈ℤ+\{g(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}} as g⁡(k)=f⁡(0)​(1−f⁡(0)1+f⁡(0))kg(k)=f(0)\left(\frac{1-f(0)}{1+f(0)}\right)^{k}. One can check that ∑k=0∞f⁡(k)=∑k=0∞g⁡(k)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}f(k)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}g(k). Note that f⁡(0)=g⁡(0)f(0)=g(0) and {g⁡(k)}k∈ℤ+\{g(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}} is a log-affine sequence. We have the majorization of {f⁡(k)}k∈ℤ+\{f(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}} over {g⁡(k)}k∈ℤ+\{g(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}. We apply Karamata’s inequality (4.1) to obtain

∑k∈ℤf​(k)2\displaystyle\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)^{2} =2​∑k∈ℤ+f​(k)2−f​(0)2≥2​∑k∈ℤ+g​(k)2−f​(0)2\displaystyle=2\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}f(k)^{2}-f(0)^{2}\geq 2\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}g(k)^{2}-f(0)^{2}
=1+f​(0)22⋅f⁡(0)>f⁡(0)2.\displaystyle=\frac{1+f(0)^{2}}{2}\cdot f(0)>\frac{f(0)}{2}.

The above inequality, together with the symmetry of X−X~X-\tilde{X}, implies that

H∞​((X−X~)+(Y−Y~))\displaystyle H_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})+(Y-\tilde{Y})) =−log(f∗f)(0)=−log∑k∈ℤf(k)2\displaystyle=-\log(f\ast f)(0)=-\log\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)^{2}
<−log⁡f⁡(0)+log⁡2=H∞​(X−X~)+log⁡2.\displaystyle<-\log f(0)+\log 2=H_{\infty}(X-\tilde{X})+\log 2. (4.3)

Observe that for any i.i.d. discrete log-concave random variables UU and VV, it holds that H2​(U)=H∞​(U−V)H_{2}(U)=H_{\infty}(U-V). We have

H2​(X+Y)\displaystyle H_{2}(X+Y) =H∞​((X+Y)−(X~+Y~))\displaystyle=H_{\infty}((X+Y)-(\tilde{X}+\tilde{Y}))
=H∞​((X−X~)+(Y−Y~))\displaystyle=H_{\infty}((X-\tilde{X})+(Y-\tilde{Y}))
<H∞​(X−X~)+log⁡2\displaystyle<H_{\infty}(X-\tilde{X})+\log 2
=H2​(X)+log⁡2.\displaystyle=H_{2}(X)+\log 2.

The inequality follows from (4.3). The moreover part is addressed later in Remark 4.4. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Similar to the continuous case, the identity H2​(X+Y)=H2​(X−Y)H_{2}(X+Y)=H_{2}(X-Y) holds for any ℤ\mathbb{Z}-valued i.i.d log-concave random variables XX and YY. Hence, Proposition 4.1 is the same as the p=2p=2 case of Theorem 2.11 of Melbourne and Palafox-Castillo [14].

Theorem 4.3.

Let XX and YY be i.i.d. log-concave random variables on ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Assume that their probability mass function ff is monotone. It holds that

‖f∗f‖∞>e−1​‖f‖∞.\|f\ast f\|_{\infty}>e^{-1}\|f\|_{\infty}.

Moreover, the inequality can not be improved. In other words, we have

H∞​(X+Y)<H∞​(X)+1.H_{\infty}(X+Y)<H_{\infty}(X)+1.
Proof.

We assume that ff is non-increasing and supported on ℤ+\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Write f⁡(k)=e−V⁡(k)f(k)=e^{-V(k)}, where VV is non-decreasing and convex. Hence, ‖f‖∞=e−V⁡(0)\|f\|_{\infty}=e^{-V(0)}. We apply the convexity of VV to obtain

(f∗f)​(k)\displaystyle(f\ast f)(k) =∑i=0ke−[V⁡(i)+V⁡(k−i)]≥∑i=0ke−[V⁡(0)+V⁡(k)]=(k+1)​e−V⁡(k)⋅‖f‖∞.\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k}e^{-[V(i)+V(k-i)]}\geq\sum_{i=0}^{k}e^{-[V(0)+V(k)]}=(k+1)e^{-V(k)}\cdot\|f\|_{\infty}.

Write ϕ⁡(k):=(k+1)​e−V⁡(k)=elog⁡(k+1)−V⁡(k)\phi(k):=(k+1)e^{-V(k)}=e^{\log(k+1)-V(k)}. It suffices to show that

supk∈ℤ+ϕ⁡(k)>1/e.\sup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\phi(k)>1/e. (4.4)

Since ϕ\phi is log-concave, the supremum in (4.4) can be achieved, say at k=k∗k=k^{*}. Consider the following scenarios.

Case 1: k∗=0k^{*}=0. Then it is necessary to have ϕ⁡(0)≥ϕ⁡(1)\phi(0)\geq\phi(1), which can be rewritten as

V⁡(1)−V⁡(0)≥log⁡2.V(1)-V(0)\geq\log 2.

Since VV is convex, it holds that

V⁡(k)≥V⁡(0)+k⁡(V⁡(1)−V⁡(0))≥V⁡(0)+k​log​2.V(k)\geq V(0)+k(V(1)-V(0))\geq V(0)+k\log 2.

As a consequence, we obtain

1=∑k=0∞f⁡(k)=e−V⁡(0)​∑k=0∞e−(V⁡(k)−V⁡(0))≤ϕ⁡(0)​∑k=0∞2−k=2​ϕ​(0).1=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}f(k)=e^{-V(0)}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-(V(k)-V(0))}\leq\phi(0)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}2^{-k}=2\phi(0).

Hence, it is necessary to have ϕ⁡(0)≥1/2\phi(0)\geq 1/2 and inequality (4.4) holds.

Case 2: k∗≥1k^{*}\geq 1. Then it is necessary to have ϕ⁡(k∗−1)≤ϕ⁡(k∗)\phi(k^{*}-1)\leq\phi(k^{*}) and ϕ⁡(k∗+1)≤ϕ⁡(k∗)\phi(k^{*}+1)\leq\phi(k^{*}), which can be rewritten as

V⁡(k∗)−V⁡(k∗−1)\displaystyle V(k^{*})-V(k^{*}-1) ≤log⁡(1+1/k∗)\displaystyle\leq\log(1+1/k^{*})
V⁡(k∗+1)−V⁡(k∗)\displaystyle V(k^{*}+1)-V(k^{*}) ≥log⁡(1+1/(k∗+1)).\displaystyle\geq\log(1+1/(k^{*}+1)).

Owing to the convexity of VV, we obtain for k≤k∗k\leq k^{*} that

V⁡(k)\displaystyle V(k) ≥V⁡(k∗)−(k∗−k)​[V⁡(k∗)−V⁡(k∗−1)]\displaystyle\geq V(k^{*})-(k^{*}-k)[V(k^{*})-V(k^{*}-1)]
≥V⁡(k∗)+(k−k∗)​log⁡(1+1/k∗)\displaystyle\geq V(k^{*})+(k-k^{*})\log(1+1/k^{*}) (4.5)

and for k≥k∗k\geq k^{*} that

V⁡(k)\displaystyle V(k) ≥V⁡(k∗)+(k−k∗)​[V⁡(k∗+1)−V⁡(k∗)]\displaystyle\geq V(k^{*})+(k-k^{*})[V(k^{*}+1)-V(k^{*})]
≥V⁡(k∗)+(k−k∗)​log⁡(1+1/(k∗+1)).\displaystyle\geq V(k^{*})+(k-k^{*})\log(1+1/(k^{*}+1)). (4.6)

Apply the estimates (4.5) and (4.6) to obtain

1=∑k=0∞f⁡(k)\displaystyle 1=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}f(k) ≤e−V⁡(k∗)​(∑k=0k∗(1+1k∗)k∗−k+∑k=k∗+1∞(1+1k∗+1)−(k−k∗))\displaystyle\leq e^{-V(k^{*})}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{k^{*}}\left(1+\frac{1}{k^{*}}\right)^{k^{*}-k}+\sum_{k=k^{*}+1}^{\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{k^{*}+1}\right)^{-(k-k^{*})}\right)
=e−V⁡(k∗)​(1+k∗​(1+1k∗)k∗+1)\displaystyle=e^{-V(k^{*})}\left(1+k^{*}\left(1+\frac{1}{k^{*}}\right)^{k^{*}+1}\right)
=ϕ⁡(k∗)​(1k∗+1+(1+1k∗)k∗)\displaystyle=\phi(k^{*})\left(\frac{1}{k^{*}+1}+\left(1+\frac{1}{k^{*}}\right)^{k^{*}}\right)
<e​ϕ​(k∗).\displaystyle<e\phi(k^{*}).

In the last inequality, we use the fact that (x+1)−1+(1+1/x)x↗e(x+1)^{-1}+(1+1/x)^{x}\nearrow e as x→∞x\rightarrow\infty. Hence, it is necessary to have ϕ⁡(k∗)>1/e\phi(k^{*})>1/e, i.e., inequality (4.4) holds. ∎

Remark 4.4.

Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.3 are tight for geometric distributions f⁡(k)=(1−λ)​λkf(k)=(1-\lambda)\lambda^{k} for k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. One can check that (f∗f)​(k)=(k+1)​(1−λ)2​λk(f\ast f)(k)=(k+1)(1-\lambda)^{2}\lambda^{k} and that
